c.tagline: World wine capital of grand 18th-century stone and a mirrored quay.

taxi.fareNote: Official taxis are metered and marked by a lit roof sign; app-booking via Uber, Bolt, or FreeNow works well throughout the city.

emergency.note: 112 is the EU-wide emergency number connecting to police, fire, and ambulance.

avoid.reason: Pickpocketing around Gare Saint-Jean and the Saint-Michel district

hood_desc: The medieval heart between the Grosse Cloche and the river, a maze of pedestrian lanes and wine bars steps from the Place de la Bourse and its mirrored Miroir d'eau; the best walkable base for first-timers.
The former wine-merchant district turned bobo-chic quarter, with antique shops, art galleries, a Sunday quayside market, and trendy cafes strung along the Garonne.
The 'golden triangle' of grand 18th-century facades between the Grand Théâtre, Cours de l'Intendance, and Allées de Tourny, home to luxury boutiques and smart cafes.
A multicultural, bohemian quarter around the soaring Flèche Saint-Michel and its flea market, full of cheap eats and a buzzing, diverse atmosphere.
An upscale, calm residential area near the Jardin Public and the Roman ruins of the Palais Gallien, lined with elegant townhouses; a quiet base.

water.note: Tap water is safe to drink, though some prefer bottled for taste.

transit.hours: Trams run from around 5am to about 1am (later on weekends); a handful of Nuit night-bus lines cover late nights.
transit.pay: TBM tickets and the reloadable TBM card are sold at machines and tabacs; a single ticket is €1.80 (about US$2), valid one hour with transfers, and contactless bank cards can buy tickets at tram machines. A day pass is around €5.

transit.m: Tram line A to the city center, ~45 min
30'Direct shuttle bus to Saint-Jean station, 30 min

tip.r: Service is included by law ('service compris'); rounding up or leaving ~5-10% for good service is appreciated but not expected.

landmarks: Place de la Bourse and Miroir d'Eau
Bordeaux's eighteenth-century riverside masterpiece doubles itself in the world's largest reflecting pool, a shallow mirror where children splash beneath golden stone facades.
La Cité du Vin
A swirling gold decanter of a building dedicated to the world's wine cultures, capped by a panoramic tasting belvedere over the Garonne.
Cathédrale Saint-André and Tour Pey-Berland
Where Eleanor of Aquitaine wed in 1137, this Gothic cathedral pairs with a free-standing bell tower whose 229 steps unveil all Bordeaux.
Grosse Cloche
One of France's oldest belfries, this fifteenth-century gate with its 7,750-kilo bell once rang to announce the grape harvest and city emergencies.
Porte Cailhau
A fairy-tale 1495 city gate of turrets and slate spires, built to honor King Charles VIII, guarding the old riverfront entrance to town.
Grand Théâtre
Victor Louis's colonnaded 1780 opera house, crowned by twelve stone muses and graces, epitomizes the neoclassical elegance that earned Bordeaux UNESCO status.
Pont de Pierre
Napoleon's graceful 17-arch brick-and-stone bridge of 1822, one arch for each letter of his name, frames the classic view of the crescent-shaped quays.
Rue Sainte-Catherine
Europe's longest pedestrian shopping street runs 1.2 kilometers from the Grand Théâtre to Place de la Victoire, threading the heart of the old town.
Basilique Saint-Michel
This UNESCO-listed Flamboyant Gothic basilica on the pilgrim route to Compostela boasts a separate 114-meter spire, the tallest in southern France.
Jardin Public
An eighteenth-century landscaped garden of swan ponds, centuries-old trees and a botanical garden, the green lung where Bordelais families promenade on Sundays.

train.note: Gare de Bordeaux Saint-Jean is about 3 km southeast of the centre, ten minutes by tram C or D. TGV inOui and Ouigo trains reach Paris Montparnasse in just over 2 hours on the LGV Sud Europe Atlantique, with Intercites and TER services to Toulouse, Marseille, Bayonne and Biarritz. There is no direct international train: for Spain take the TER to Hendaye and change at Irun, which usually adds two changes and most of a day to a Bordeaux-San Sebastian trip. Ouigo tickets are sold only on ouigo.com and SNCF Connect and are non-flexible, so check the terms before booking.

bus.note: Long-distance coaches leave from the stops on Rue Charles Domercq and Rue des Terres de Borde beside Saint-Jean station, southeast of the centre. Because there is no through train to Spain, the coach is the practical surface option: Bilbao takes about 4h30m and San Sebastian about 3h30m. Book online in advance - there is no ticket office, and the exact stop is printed on the ticket, so check it as the kerbside positions move. Regional Nouvelle-Aquitaine services are branded Cars Regionaux and are bought on board or through SNCF Connect.

intl.to: Lormont, Bassens, Les Hangars & Stalingrad (France) - Garonne river shuttle from the quays in the centre

ferry.note: Bordeaux is a river port 100 km up the Garonne from the sea, so its only scheduled boats are the Bat3 river shuttles run by the city transport network TBM, which cross and run along the river using ordinary tram tickets. Cruise ships tie up at the Quai des Chartrons and Quai Louis XVIII in the centre, and Gironde estuary excursion boats run in summer. There are no international ferries - the nearest are Brittany Ferries' sailings from Bilbao and Santander (https://www.brittany-ferries.co.uk/) or from Saint-Malo and Roscoff further north.
